US consumer confidence is collapsing.

The Consumer Confidence Index dropped -6.7 points in September, to 81.9, its lowest since April 2014.

This marks its 4th consecutive monthly decline, totaling -11.2 points.

The Present Situation Index fell -7.9 points, to 109.3, its lowest since February 2021.

At the same time, the Expectations Index fell -5.9 points, to 63.6, its lowest since April 2025, marking its 3rd consecutive monthly decline.

Over the last 6 months, confidence across all age groups and nearly all income groups has declined.

Consumers are also increasingly citing high prices, the cost of goods and services, and oil and gasoline prices as major factors weighing on the economy.

Overall, the US is undergoing a transition in its marginal source of financing.

Some traditional foreign reserve buyers are becoming less reliable:

-Japan because currency defence can require dollar liquidity.
-China because of long-term reserve diversification.
-Europe because incremental Treasury buying has weakened.

Meanwhile, the marginal buyer is increasingly coming from elsewhere:

-US money-market funds.
-Banks.
-The Fed.
-Private foreign investors.
-And increasingly, stablecoins.

The debt can still be financed.

The more important question is what yield the US must offer to continuously attract that changing marginal buyer and if US gov led buying would only increase the issue of

But the scale needs perspective.

In 2025:

-Foreign investors bought roughly $545B of Treasuries.
-US money-market funds bought roughly $523B.
-Mutual funds + ETFs bought ~$256B.
-Households bought ~$249B.
-US banks bought ~$179B.

Against that, the measured increase in outright Treasury exposure from Tether + USDC was roughly $23B.

Growing quickly. But so far nowhere near large enough yet to solve the Treasury financing problem.

Given the recent bond moves, I spent some time trying to understand what is actually happening underneath the US Treasury market.

The common narrative is that there are “no buyers” for US debt.

That isn't quite right.

The more interesting story is that the composition of the buyer base is changing at exactly the same time that the US needs to finance enormous amounts of debt.
